newsitem.title: USA: Rumpled, good-humored Berger made key Clinton aide.
newsitem.headline: Rumpled, good-humored Berger made key Clinton aide.

text.p: Samuel "Sandy" Berger, picked to become President Bill Clinton's new national security adviser, is a rumpled, good-humoured man with a keen political eye who works out of an office about the size of a jail cell.
Berger, 51, is seen by his colleagues as a quick decision maker with a tight focus who works well in a small group where fostering consensus and drawing out opinions is at a premium.

Berger has been deputy national security adviser throughout Clinton's first term. He will take over from Anthony Lake, who largely shied away from taking a public role explaining and defending Clinton's foreign policy.

The choice of Berger was welcomed by many White House officials who believed he would be more media-savvy than Lake. There have been reports that Berger chafed privately at being the number two under Lake in coordinating U.S. foreign policy from the White House.
With a background as a trade lawyer, Berger is seen as an expert on the relationship between economics, diplomacy and military power. His top areas of interest have been Asia and South Asia.

Around the West Wing, he is known as an often-rumpled character with good humour who is prone to the occasional temper explosion, typical of most power people in Washington. His life is one of many meetings.

Long active in Democratic politics, Berger sat in on the weekly political brainstorming sessions Clinton held with top advisers in the White House residence during his re-election campaign. He attended the Democratic convention in Chicago, although Lake did not out of fears he would be seen as too political.
But aides say Berger does not make foreign policy decisions based on political concerns. "He has a political role and he has a foreign policy role and they are separate," said one.
Berger's office is a 10-by-10 foot square, a small but coveted space in the West Wing, and he can be found there at lunchtime usually eating a meal retrieved from the White House mess.
"It has more distance from floor to ceiling than it does from side to side," said one aide of the Berger office.
Otherwise, he can be found either in Lake's office, Clinton's Oval Office, or in the Situation Room downstairs monitoring diplomatic cables and intelligence reports coming in from around the world.
Like Clinton, Berger worked on the failed campaign of Democrat George McGovern to oust Richard Nixon from the White House in 1972.
He was a deputy director of President Jimmy Carter's State Department policy planning staff from 1977-1980.
Berger is also comfortable on Capitol Hill, where he has worked for Sen. Harold Hughes of Iowa and Representative Joseph Resnick of New York, among others.
He received an undergraduate degree from Cornell University in 1967 and a law degree from Harvard in 1971.

He has written a book on American rural politics, "Dollar Harvest," and has campaigned on human rights issues. He was assistant director of Clinton's transition team for national security issues in 1992.
Berger is married to Susan Harrison Berger and has three children, Deborah, 20, Sarah, 15, and Alexander, 13.
